lvl-cap-ngs: Standard geodetic levelling (NGS-style): 60 m balanced sights. At 60 m the curvature correction is a mere 0.3 mm per sight — and because back-sight and fore-sight distances are kept equal, it cancels exactly between the two staff readings. The procedure is DESIGNED around the curve: short sights, balanced setups, thousands of times per line. On a flat earth none of this discipline would buy anything.
lvl-cap-bedford: Wallace's three-marker design on the Old Bedford River (9.7 km), 1870. Three markers at equal height above the water; one sight line joining the end markers. The sphere predicts the middle marker stands proud of that line by d²/8R ≈ 1.85 m — about 1.6 m after standard refraction — and through Wallace's telescope, it did. Drawn with the vertical scale exaggerated (factor printed); the metres are true.
lvl-cap-pontchartrain: A 38.4 km chord across Lake Pontchartrain. Stretch a straight line between two shore points 38.4 km apart and the level water surface bulges d²/8R ≈ 29 m above its midpoint — which is why the far end of the causeway, its pilings and its traffic sink below the horizon in every long-lens photograph, bottom first. The flat prediction is a bulge of exactly zero.
lvl-cap-rainylake: Rainy Lake, Minnesota–Ontario, spring 2018 — the Bedford Level redone with GPS. Targets planted on a metre of lake ice out to 9.5 km, each one fixed to centimetres by differential GPS, and the observer's line of sight compared against both models. Same three-marker logic as Wallace, but with the positions measured rather than argued about: the surface came out curved at roughly 6,400 km radius.
lvl-cap-suez: The Suez Canal, 162 km of lock-free water. A standing flat-earth argument is that the canal was dug level and therefore proves a flat sea. It proves the opposite: “level” means following an equipotential, and a straight chord between its ends would pass d²/8R ≈ 515 m below the midpoint of the water surface. Nobody dug a chord — the surveyors levelled, which is a curvature-following procedure.
lvl-cap-ligo: A 4 km laser arm that had to be built as a chord. The beam tube of a gravitational-wave interferometer is straight because light is; the ground under it is not. Over 4 km the surface falls about 1.25 m away from the straight tube, and the concrete had to be graded to match. The instrument would not have worked if the correction had been left out.

exp7-verd: Verdict rule: plot your readings against d². A flat earth is vindicated by a flat line at zero. The globe requires a straight line of slope 1/2R — about 6.8 cm per km² through changing weather (refraction moves it a few percent, never to zero, never negative on average). Wallace's three-marker variant needs just one observation: does the middle marker stand proud of the end-to-end line, by d²/8R? In 1870 it did, and it still does.
